notes: “The way of all the earth” pictures death as the journey everyone takes. David’s next commands connect wisdom with both loyalty and executions.
David recalls his oath not to kill Shimei, then tells Solomon to bring him down to Sheol in blood. The translation leaves that tension in place.
Solomon’s last words abruptly name Adonijah, Abiathar, and Joab together. The Hebrew does not spell out a new conspiracy.
The pinned Hebrew says Joab had not followed Absalom. It is not changed to Solomon.
The warning names crossing the Kidron, while Shimei later goes to Gath. Verse 36 also forbids leaving Jerusalem for any destination; the wording of each instruction is preserved.
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead. “Gray head” keeps the image of an old man going down to death.
House
Here a continuing royal family or dynasty; elsewhere in Kings the same word refers to a palace or the temple.
Horns of the altar
Projections at the altar’s corners. Joab holds them while seeking refuge, as Adonijah did in chapter 1.

sections.16: Two women and one living child

notes: “A young boy” is Solomon’s self-description. “Go out or come in” can describe conducting one’s responsibilities; it does not supply his age.
A “listening heart” joins attention, discernment, and judgment. In biblical Hebrew the heart includes thought and decision, not only feeling.
The account that the other woman lay on her son is the first woman’s testimony. It is not a separate statement by the narrator.
“The first woman” identifies the woman who asked that the living child be spared in verse 26; the Hebrew says “her.”
vocabulary: High places
Worship sites, often on heights. The account distinguishes the lack of a temple from its assessment of Solomon’s worship.
Fellowship offerings
Sacrifices associated with shared well-being and a meal; the Hebrew term is related to shalom, peace or wholeness.

notes: “The priest” can be read as Azariah’s office or as identifying his father Zadok. The brief list leaves the attachment open.
Abiathar remains in this list of priests, although chapter 2 describes his removal. The list is not silently reconciled with that narrative.
The final clause says there was one official in that land. Its relation to Geber’s district is unclear; “Judah” is not supplied.
These public verse labels correspond to Hebrew 5:1–14 in the pinned source. The complete words and order are preserved.
The pinned Hebrew gives forty thousand stalls and twelve thousand horsemen. These numbers are retained.
“A breadth of heart” pictures expansive understanding. The sand image also describes Israel’s population in verse 20.
vocabulary: The River
The Euphrates, the great river marking the reach of Solomon’s rule in this description.
Cor
An ancient measure of capacity used here for flour. The original quantities are retained without imposing an exact modern conversion.

notes: This chapter corresponds to Hebrew 5:15–32 in the pinned source.
“My feet” follows the source’s read form. Its written form has “his feet,” referring back to David.
The source specifies twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of beaten olive oil each year.
Israel’s thirty thousand men serve in rotating forced-labor shifts. Chapter 9:22 distinguishes Israelites from those Solomon made slaves; the two descriptions are both retained.
This passage gives 3,300 supervisors. Chapter 9:23 gives 550 chief officials; the translation does not replace either count.
vocabulary: Cypress
A conventional identification of the Hebrew timber name; the exact tree species is uncertain.
Covenant
A binding agreement, here between Solomon and Hiram.
Gebalites
People of Gebal, named alongside Solomon’s and Hiram’s builders.

sections.14: The inner rooms and their decoration

notes: The compressed description of the windows is uncertain. “Recessed frames” is an architectural interpretation, not a recoverable construction drawing.
The pinned Hebrew calls this the entrance to the middle story, then describes going up to the middle story. Both references are retained.
The Hebrew here reads “from the floor up to the walls.” Unlike verse 15, it does not explicitly name the ceiling.
“Five-sided” and “four-sided” interpret the numbered doorframes. The phrases can also be taken as proportions of an opening; their precise architecture is uncertain.
The dates run from Ziv in Solomon’s fourth year to Bul in his eleventh. The narrative itself describes the building as taking seven years.
vocabulary: Cubit
A length based on the forearm. The original measurements stay visible so readers can compare the building’s proportions.
Most Holy Place
The innermost sanctuary, where the ark would be placed.
Cherubim
Winged beings represented here by large wooden figures covered with gold; the two figures’ wings reach across the sanctuary.

notes: Four rows of pillars are named, followed by forty-five beams, fifteen in a row. What the second count modifies is not wholly clear; neither number is changed.
The Hebrew says “from floor to floor.” “From one end of the floor to the other” makes a possible sense of that wording; “floor to ceiling” would require a different reading.
This account identifies Hiram’s mother with Naphtali and his father with Tyre. Hiram the craftsman is distinct from King Hiram.

The Hebrew places “pillars” and “pomegranates” awkwardly in verse 18. Exchanging the two terms would produce a smoother construction description, but the draft retains their positions. Verse 42 clearly describes the rows of pomegranates.
The Sea is described as ten cubits across, thirty around, five high, and holding two thousand baths. The translation preserves the ancient measurements as given.
The stand’s opening, crown, and panels are described with compressed pronouns. Their exact arrangement remains uncertain.
The Hebrew gives each basin a measurement of four cubits without identifying the dimension.
Verse 40 names basins; verse 45 names pots. Both source terms are retained rather than making the lists identical.
The final door fittings may be sockets or hinges; their precise form is uncertain.
vocabulary: Capital
The shaped top of a pillar.
Jachin and Boaz
The pillars’ names suggest “he establishes” and “in him is strength.” The text gives the names without an explanation.
Bath
An ancient liquid measure. The Sea and the smaller basins have distinct capacities.

notes: This account says the ark contained only the two stone tablets. No other objects are added.
Solomon’s short poetic declaration retains both thick darkness and a permanent dwelling. Verse 27 then asks how any house could contain God.
The oath invokes a curse in a dispute. Solomon asks God to judge the guilty and the innocent; the translation keeps that legal setting.
The prayer explicitly includes a foreigner from a distant land, so that all peoples may know the LORD’s name.
The prayer anticipates wrongdoing, exile, return of heart, forgiveness, and compassion from captors. It does not explicitly promise release in verse 50.
Verse 65 says seven days plus seven days, fourteen in all; verse 66 says “the eighth day.” Their relation is left as the account presents it.
vocabulary: Glory
The LORD’s overwhelming presence, here filling the house in a cloud.
Covenant
The binding relationship with Israel, represented here by the tablets in the ark.
Iron furnace
An image for Egypt as a place of intense affliction.

notes: “High as it is” keeps the pinned word for high or exalted. The text describes people’s horror without explicitly calling the house a heap of ruins.
“Tadmor” follows the source’s read form; the written form is “Tamar.” The difference affects the place being named.
The text distinguishes inherited slave labor imposed on these peoples from the Israelites’ roles. It does not erase the Israelite forced-labor levy in 5:13–14.
The final phrase can mean completing or bringing the house to its intended state. Its relation to Solomon’s continuing sacrifices is not spelled out.
The Sea of Reeds is named here beside Eloth and Ezion-geber in Edom. The geographical context is retained.
vocabulary: Millo
A named structure associated with Jerusalem’s building works; the word suggests a filled or built-up area.
Devote to destruction
Language of the ban: here it refers to destroying these peoples, not merely displacing them.
Talent
An ancient weight used for precious metal, not a coin of a fixed modern value.

notes: “Burnt offering” follows the wording’s sacrificial sense. The phrase can also be understood as Solomon’s ascent or approach to the temple.
The pinned Hebrew says “your men.” The translation retains this gendered wording.
The almug wood’s identity and the exact form of the architectural supports are uncertain.
The pinned vocalization suggests “mixed peoples.” “Arabia” is another way the underlying consonants have been understood.
The weight unit shekel is supplied with the numbers where the Hebrew leaves it unstated. Verse 17 explicitly names minas.
“Tarshish fleet” identifies the fleet, without necessarily specifying the destination of each voyage. The last cargo terms are uncertain; ivory, apes, and peacocks are conventional identifications.
“Kue” takes the disputed term as a place name. It can also be understood in connection with a gathering or company of traders.
vocabulary: Riddles
Testing questions or difficult sayings, not necessarily word games.
Mina
A unit of weight, used here for gold.
Lowland
The lower hill country contrasted with Jerusalem and the central hills.

notes: The Hebrew names Milcom in verse 5 and Molech in verse 7. These forms are preserved rather than silently made identical.
Joab’s killing of every male in Edom and Hadad’s flight as a boy are both stated. The account’s sweeping claim is not softened.
The reference to Hadad’s harm interrupts the description of Rezon. The syntax is difficult; the draft retains both adversaries and the statement that he ruled Aram.
The context most naturally identifies Ahijah as wearing the new cloak, though the Hebrew pronouns do not name the wearer again.
Twelve pieces are torn, ten offered to Jeroboam, and one tribe reserved for Solomon’s line. The uneven accounting is retained.
The source switches to plural “they” for the apostasy but ends with “David his father.” The change of number is left visible.
Jeroboam too receives a conditional promise of an enduring house. The affliction of David’s descendants is explicitly “not forever.”
vocabulary: Concubine
A woman in a recognized union with lower standing than a wife; the account distinguishes the two groups.
Adversary
Hebrew satan here describes an opponent raised against Solomon; it is not used as a personal name.
Lamp
An image of David’s continuing royal line.

notes: The pinned Hebrew says Jeroboam stayed in Egypt, then reports that the assembly sent for him. “Returned from Egypt” is not substituted in verse 2.
The elders link becoming the people’s servant, serving them, and having them as servants. The repeated word exposes the choice facing Rehoboam.
“My little finger” supplies “finger” for “my little one.” The boast contrasts it with his father’s waist; “scorpions” intensifies the image of a punishing whip.
Verse 20 names Judah alone; verse 21 names Judah and Benjamin. Both descriptions are retained.
The calf declaration echoes the wording about coming out of Egypt. The Hebrew uses a plural verb here; “gods” preserves that grammar without resolving everything the calves were meant to represent.
“His own heart” follows the source’s read form.
vocabulary: Yoke
A wooden fitting for working animals; here an image of the burdens imposed by the king.
House of David
David’s dynasty. In the people’s chant, “your own house” also turns the king’s attention back to his own concerns.

notes: The pinned Hebrew begins with one son coming, then speaks of the sons reporting. The change from singular to plural is retained.
The narrator says the old prophet lied. The same prophet subsequently receives the LORD’s word; his earlier claim and the later event remain distinct.
The Hebrew is compressed about the saddling. The draft identifies the old prophet as the one who saddles the donkey for the returning man of God.
The lion has killed the man but has eaten neither his body nor the donkey. These details are part of the report.
“The cities of Samaria” is retained even though the founding of the city named Samaria is recounted later, in chapter 16.
vocabulary: Man of God
A designation for a person speaking or acting with divine authority; here the prophet from Judah.
Ordain
The Hebrew idiom is “fill the hand,” used for installing someone in priestly service.

notes: The coarse wall-urinating expression specifically targets males. “Confined or free” renders an uncertain pair of terms that appears to include everyone in the threatened group.
The final exclamations are abrupt and difficult: “this very day,” followed by “and what? Even now!” The draft preserves the broken urgency without assigning a new date.
The Hebrew qadesh names male shrine attendants. “Male cult prostitutes” is a traditional rendering, but the word alone does not settle their sexual function.
The account describes continuing war between the kings even though 12:24 records the abandonment of one invasion. Neither statement is removed.
vocabulary: Asherah poles
Cult objects associated with Asherah; the form of a particular object is not always clear.
Records of the kings
The account refers to royal records as sources for further deeds; this title does not identify the biblical books of Chronicles.

notes: Both Abijam and Asa are associated with Maacah daughter of Abishalom as “mother.” The term can express a broader ancestral or dynastic relation; the main text does not replace it with “grandmother.”
The pinned Hebrew names Rehoboam here, even in the account of Abijam. The pronoun in “his lifetime” is not fully resolved.
“Male shrine attendants” follows the same choice as 14:24. The precise form of Maacah’s “monstrous image” for Asherah is uncertain.
Asa’s wholehearted loyalty and the survival of the high places appear side by side.
Baasha’s father Ahijah is named without identifying him as Ahijah the prophet. No such relationship is supplied.
vocabulary: Lamp
The image of a continuing royal line, also used in 11:36.
Covenant
Here a political agreement. Asa asks Ben-hadad to break one agreement in favor of another.

notes: Baasha is condemned for destroying Jeroboam’s house, although 15:29 presents that destruction as fulfilling the LORD’s word. The tension is retained.
The male-targeting idiom is retained, followed by the additional groups of relatives and friends. The violence is not reduced to a change of rulers.
The narrative gives Asa’s twenty-seventh year for Omri’s proclamation in the camp and thirty-first for this accession notice. Neither date is adjusted.
The building of Jericho is linked to the loss of Hiel’s firstborn and youngest sons. The verse does not describe how they died; the translation does not assert a child-sacrifice procedure.
vocabulary: Worthless idols
The Hebrew uses a word for emptiness or futility to characterize the objects of worship.
Samaria
The city’s name is connected here with Shemer, from whom Omri bought the hill.

notes: The pinned Hebrew identifies Elijah among the inhabitants of Gilead. It does not explicitly locate a town named Tishbe here.
The widow expects one last meal before death; Elijah asks for his portion first. The draft retains this difficult sequence rather than smoothing it into a general promise of provision.
Both the widow and Elijah address the child’s death as harm involving God. Their questions are retained as their speech.
Nefesh can mean life or a living being. “His life returned into him” follows the bodily sequence of no breath, prayer, and renewed life without imposing an account of the soul’s nature.
vocabulary: Wadi
A stream valley whose water may dry up.
Upper room
A room above the main living space, where Elijah is staying.

notes: Elijah requests 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah. The ensuing contest specifically counts Baal’s prophets. It does not separately narrate the fate of all 400 prophets of Asherah.
“Limp” connects the people’s divided allegiance with the prophets’ movement around the altar. The first phrase can picture two branches or two alternatives.
Elijah’s claim to be the only remaining prophet stands alongside the account of Obadiah hiding a hundred. It is left as Elijah’s speech.
“Relieving himself” takes a possible euphemistic sense of the Hebrew. “Occupied” or “gone aside” are less specific possibilities.
The trench is described by two seahs of seed. This may indicate its capacity or the area that amount of seed would sow.
The verse division follows the pinned Hebrew: preparing the bull in verse 33, then all three water instructions in verse 34.
The Hebrew says “you have turned their hearts back.” The direction can be heard as restoration, though turning backward or away is also possible. The perfect form is retained.
“Slaughtered” preserves the force of the verb. The account names Elijah as carrying out the killing.
vocabulary: LORD of Armies
A title presenting the LORD as commander of hosts or armies.
Grain offering
An offering of grain or flour; its customary time locates the prayer within the day.

notes: The pinned Hebrew reads “he saw,” rather than “he was afraid.” The draft says he saw what was happening and fled for his life.
The source says “the cave,” without explicitly identifying it as a cave occupied earlier by Moses.
Elijah repeats his answer word for word. The repetition is preserved rather than rewritten to sound less repetitive.

“A sound of fine stillness” keeps the unusual pairing of sound and quiet. “A gentle whisper” is another possible way to express it; the verse does not explicitly state that the LORD was in the stillness.
The renewed commission includes the swords of Hazael and Jehu and killing attributed to Elisha. These disturbing elements remain beside the care shown to Elijah.
“What have I done to you?” can be heard as release, reminder, or challenge. The question remains open.
vocabulary: Broom bush
A desert shrub giving Elijah a place to lie down.
Cloak
Elijah’s outer garment, thrown over Elisha in an action that calls him to follow.

notes: The division follows the pinned Hebrew: the messengers are sent in verse 2, and their message is given in verse 3.
The Hebrew adjective “finest” or “best” follows “wives and sons”; its scope may include both groups.
The Arameans’ claim about gods of hills is their explanation for defeat. The later prophetic answer specifically names the LORD. The voices are kept distinct.
The account gives one hundred thousand foot soldiers killed in one day and twenty-seven thousand men under the falling wall. These large numbers are preserved.
The source places the ropes on their heads, without specifying how they were worn. It is not changed to “around their necks.”
The exchange switches speakers without naming them. The draft identifies Ben-hadad’s offer and Ahab’s release terms; “trading streets” interprets the streets as a commercial concession.
The word here denotes a bandage or head covering, not ashes.
The prophet calls Ben-hadad a man devoted to destruction. The chapter has not previously quoted an order to Ahab using those words.
vocabulary: Company of prophets
Literally “sons of the prophets,” expressing membership in a prophetic group.
Talent of silver
A substantial weight of silver demanded as the alternative to the guard’s life; it is not converted into modern currency.

notes: Naboth appeals to his ancestral inheritance. Ahab’s retelling to Jezebel leaves that reason out and reports only a refusal to give up the vineyard.
Jezebel’s words about Ahab exercising kingship can be read as a taunting question or as an assertion. The draft uses a question.
The Hebrew uses “bless” euphemistically where the accusation requires “curse.” The witnesses’ charge is part of the arranged killing, not the narrator’s finding against Naboth.
The charge joins murder with taking possession. The precise place named for the blood repayment is kept without harmonizing it with later accounts.
The coarse male-targeting idiom recurs from 14:10 and 16:11. “Confined or free” preserves the uncertain inclusive pair.
The pinned form is rendered “rampart.” It is not silently replaced with a different word for plot or district.
The narrative describes Ahab’s actions and the LORD’s recognition of his humbling. The disaster is deferred to his son’s days, not canceled.
vocabulary: Inheritance
Land received through one’s family, with obligations and identity beyond its sale price.
Fast
Abstaining from food; here Jezebel uses a public fast as the setting for the accusation.
Sackcloth
Coarse cloth worn as an outward sign of mourning or humbling.
